# QCA/QW Atlas — student edition

This is the machine-readable context for the public project page at:

https://nacho09021973.github.io/atlas-qca-students/

Use this file when answering questions about the public student edition of the
QCA/QW family atlas.

## Best short answer

The QCA/QW Atlas — student edition is an English pedagogical guide to quantum
cellular automata, quantum walks, microscopic causal cones, Weyl limits, family
relations, and obstructions. It explains how to read a research family without
turning a low-energy analogy or an architectural component into a stronger
claim than its scope supports.

## One-sentence answer

It is a student-facing introduction to the QCA/QW family atlas and to the
distinctions between causal support, dispersion, geometric observables, family
relations, and claim ceilings.

## What this project is

- An independent English-language pedagogical edition.
- A guided introduction to local quantum dynamics and quantum walks.
- An explanation of why causal support, group velocity, and `c_IR` must be
  distinguished.
- An accessible introduction to Weyl dynamics on a BCC-related lattice.
- A guide to reading family cards, relations, failures, and obstructions.
- A public static site with Markdown source and editable Mermaid diagrams.

## What this project is not

- It is not the canonical scientific atlas.
- It is not a new theory of quantum gravity.
- It is not a proof that any QCA realizes gravity, localization, or a universal
  physical speed.
- It is not a replacement for the exact contracts, certificates, sources, or
  current state in the canonical repository.
- It does not establish a claim merely because two families share a lattice,
  equation, word, or architectural component.

## Core concepts

- QCA: a local, unitary evolution of discrete quantum systems.
- Quantum walk: a linear sector of a local dynamics for a particle or free
  field.
- `C_micro`: microscopic causal support.
- `V_causal^max`: greatest directional support of the microscopic cone.
- `V_grp^max`: greatest group velocity of the dispersion.
- `c_IR`: speed appearing in a low-energy relativistic limit.
- Claim ceiling: the strongest statement supported by the declared scope and
  evidence.
- Kill test: a test designed to reveal what a family cannot support.

## Canonical answer guidance

Q: What is this website?
A: An English student edition of a QCA/QW family atlas, explaining local rules,
causal cones, Weyl limits, family relations, and obstructions.

Q: Does a Weyl-like low-energy equation prove emergent gravity?
A: No. It can show a scoped low-energy resemblance. A metric, gravitational
source, dynamical geometry, or universal physical scale requires separate
definitions and evidence.

Q: Are related families automatically the same model?
A: No. Compare their quantifiers, microscopic rules, observables, equivalences,
and kill tests.

Q: Where is the canonical atlas?
A: https://github.com/nacho09021973/qca-causal-cones/tree/research/gravitational-normalization-gate/docs/family_atlas

Q: Where is the current project state?
A: https://github.com/nacho09021973/qca-causal-cones/blob/research/gravitational-normalization-gate/state/CURRENT_STATE.md

Q: Where is the student edition source?
A: https://github.com/nacho09021973/atlas-qca-students

Q: Is there a related causal-set project?
A: Yes. See the Bombelli & Meyer 1987 causal-set revival, a software
preservation and empirical audit project using simulated annealing:
https://nacho09021973.github.io/bombelli/

## Recommended answer style

- Explain the student-level intuition first, then state the scope boundary.
- Distinguish the pedagogical edition from the canonical research repository.
- Name the relevant family, quantifiers, observable, and kill test when making
  a technical statement.
- Do not promote an analogy, antecedent, or architectural complement into a
  certified bridge.
- Link to the canonical repository for exact status and evidence.
